---
title: "Geographies of Climate Learning"
description: "How does place shape which urban climate knowledge is produced, recognised and useful elsewhere?"
canonical-url: "/research/geographies-of-climate-learning.html"
---

<!-- Generated by scripts/generate_site.py; do not edit. -->

Cities cannot investigate every climate question independently, so urban climate decisions necessarily draw on studies, models, cases and practical experience produced elsewhere. Yet research and policy often treat the existence of a precedent, or a visible resemblance between two cities, as evidence that its lessons will travel. That inference is uncertain. Institutional arrangements, infrastructure, climate, political authority, fiscal capacity, data systems and social conditions may alter what another city can plausibly learn.

Geographies of Climate Learning examines where urban climate knowledge is produced, which cities and populations are made visible, how particular places become influential reference cases, and which institutions recognise some forms of evidence as authoritative. It also follows evidence as it moves: how findings are interpreted, adapted, combined, contested or rejected in new settings. The aim is not to identify universally transferable lessons, but to understand what would have to be true for evidence produced in one place to become informative in another.

::: {.what-this-changes}
**The proposition.** Cross-city learning is not simply a search for the most similar city. It is a judgement about which contextual differences matter for the decision at hand.
:::

**What this theme does not assume.** This theme concerns existing knowledge and the conditions under which it may be relevant elsewhere. It does not presume that proximity, similarity or the volume of available research establishes applicability.

## Questions this theme opens

These are possible directions for future research, not active or funded projects.

<span class="sr-only">Each card retains the full status: Research idea · not currently an active or funded project</span>

This layout provides a reading hierarchy; it is not a ranking of research priority, funding readiness or importance.

```{=html}
<h3 class="idea-group-heading">Questions at the centre of this theme</h3><div class="idea-grid signature-grid"><article class="idea-card signature-idea" data-narrative-tier="signature"><p class="idea-badge">Research idea</p><p class="sr-only">Research idea · not currently an active or funded project</p><h3>When similarity misleads</h3><p class="idea-question">Which contextual differences cause apparently comparable cities to draw different policy conclusions from the same evidence?</p><h4>Why this question matters</h4><p>Cities often select precedents through visible similarities such as population, climate or income, even though less visible institutional and infrastructural differences may alter the result. Analogue-based learning can create misplaced confidence when the characteristics used to define similarity are not the characteristics that govern the intervention or outcome.</p><h4>How we might study it</h4><p>Matched-city comparisons could be combined with causal transportability analysis and sensitivity testing to identify which contextual variables alter the direction or magnitude of an inference.</p><ul class="method-list"><li>matched-city comparison</li><li>transportability analysis</li><li>causal generalisability</li></ul><p class="idea-reader"><strong>Reader or decision at stake:</strong> Comparative researchers selecting cases.</p></article><article class="idea-card signature-idea" data-narrative-tier="signature"><p class="idea-badge">Research idea</p><p class="sr-only">Research idea · not currently an active or funded project</p><h3>Evidence in translation</h3><p class="idea-question">How is urban climate evidence changed as it moves through city networks, consultancies, policy guidance and local decision processes?</p><h4>Why this question matters</h4><p>Cities rarely encounter research in its original scholarly form, yet little is known about how claims and limitations change as evidence is translated into guidance and plans. Simplification or reframing may detach findings from the conditions under which they were produced and create stronger policy claims than the original evidence supports.</p><h4>How we might study it</h4><p>Document-lineage analysis and text-similarity methods could trace changes between papers, guidance, consultancy reports and municipal plans, while interviews could explain why particular claims were retained or altered.</p><ul class="method-list"><li>document-lineage analysis</li><li>text similarity</li><li>natural-language processing</li></ul><p class="idea-reader"><strong>Reader or decision at stake:</strong> Policy intermediaries and evidence-synthesis teams.</p></article></div><h3 class="idea-group-heading">Additional directions</h3><div class="idea-grid"><article class="idea-card" data-narrative-tier="additional"><p class="idea-badge">Research idea</p><p class="sr-only">Research idea · not currently an active or funded project</p><h3>Who becomes a reference city?</h3><p class="idea-question">How do a small number of cities become influential reference cases, and how does their prominence shape what other cities regard as feasible?</p><h4>Why this question matters</h4><p>The most visible city cases may become influential because they are well documented or internationally connected rather than because their experience is broadly informative. Reliance on a small set of reference cities may narrow which policy pathways appear credible and reproduce the existing geography of urban climate knowledge.</p><h4>How we might study it</h4><p>Citation-network analysis, city-network records and policy-document tracing could reconstruct how particular cases acquire authority and how their lessons are reproduced in guidance and municipal plans.</p><ul class="method-list"><li>citation-network analysis</li><li>policy-document tracing</li><li>network analysis</li></ul><p class="idea-reader"><strong>Reader or decision at stake:</strong> Researchers and policy intermediaries selecting precedents.</p></article><article class="idea-card" data-narrative-tier="additional"><p class="idea-badge">Research idea</p><p class="sr-only">Research idea · not currently an active or funded project</p><h3>The missing geography of failure</h3><p class="idea-question">Are abandoned, reversed or unsuccessful urban climate interventions systematically absent from the evidence available to other cities?</p><h4>Why this question matters</h4><p>Urban climate learning often relies on celebrated or completed cases, while abandoned and reversed interventions remain difficult to locate. A learning system built mainly from visible successes may overestimate feasibility and conceal the political or institutional conditions under which action fails.</p><h4>How we might study it</h4><p>A registry of discontinued and unsuccessful initiatives, combined with archival research and comparative process tracing, could test whether documented success cases differ systematically from the wider population of interventions.</p><ul class="method-list"><li>archival research</li><li>case-registry development</li><li>comparative process tracing</li></ul><p class="idea-reader"><strong>Reader or decision at stake:</strong> Researchers building comparative evidence bases.</p></article><article class="idea-card" data-narrative-tier="additional"><p class="idea-badge">Research idea</p><p class="sr-only">Research idea · not currently an active or funded project</p><h3>Whose knowledge becomes admissible?</h3><p class="idea-question">How do urban evidence systems recognise, subordinate or exclude Indigenous, community and practitioner knowledge?</p><h4>Why this question matters</h4><p>Formal evidence hierarchies may exclude locally authoritative knowledge or incorporate it without preserving control over interpretation and use. Decisions may overlook place-specific conditions, while extractive forms of inclusion may reproduce inequities in who owns and authorises knowledge.</p><h4>How we might study it</h4><p>Co-designed comparative research, undertaken only with appropriate partners and data-sovereignty arrangements, could examine how institutions define admissible evidence and how those rules affect decisions.</p><p class="idea-qualification"><strong>Research governance qualification.</strong> Methods and research governance would need to be developed with appropriate Indigenous or community partners rather than specified unilaterally in advance.</p><ul class="method-list"><li>co-designed research</li><li>institutional ethnography</li><li>knowledge-system mapping</li></ul><p class="idea-reader"><strong>Reader or decision at stake:</strong> Community or Indigenous partners and evidence-governance researchers.</p></article><article class="idea-card" data-narrative-tier="additional"><p class="idea-badge">Research idea</p><p class="sr-only">Research idea · not currently an active or funded project</p><h3>AI-selected urban analogues</h3><p class="idea-question">When AI systems are asked which cities are comparable, which places do they recommend and which contextual differences do they ignore?</p><h4>Why this question matters</h4><p>AI-assisted discovery may increasingly shape which urban precedents researchers and practitioners encounter, but the geographical and contextual biases of those comparisons remain poorly understood. AI-generated analogues may reproduce existing evidence concentrations or recommend superficially similar cities while overlooking the conditions that determine relevance.</p><h4>How we might study it</h4><p>Controlled prompt experiments, counterfactual city profiles and expert assessment could test the stability, geographical concentration and contextual adequacy of AI-generated city comparisons.</p><ul class="method-list"><li>controlled model experiments</li><li>counterfactual city profiles</li><li>audit studies</li></ul><p class="idea-reader"><strong>Reader or decision at stake:</strong> Researchers and practitioners using AI-assisted discovery.</p></article></div>
```

## How this connects

- **Input from [Consequences for People and Places](/research/consequences-for-people-and-places.html):** Observed consequences generate new knowledge, expose the limits of earlier assumptions and change what other cities may plausibly learn.
- **Next stage — [Where New Evidence Matters](/research/where-new-evidence-matters.html):** Mapping the reach and limits of existing knowledge reveals which unresolved questions could be consequential enough to justify new research.
- **Return loop:** Consequences generate new evidence, reveal unresolved questions and revise what other cities may plausibly learn.
